text: They grew up on a dry farm at the edge of the desert, where the family paid raiders each harvest to be left alone. One year the family could not pay, and the raiders burned the fields. One sibling stayed to rebuild, and they left to find work in the towns.
They were sold to a mining camp young and spent years under the whip. They saved cats one at a time and bought their freedom. They walked out of the camp gate with nothing but the clothes they wore.

They were drafted into a holy army and marched for years in the name of a god they never felt. When their unit was ordered to burn a village, they walked away in the night. No one came after them, and they never saw that unit again.

They grew up on scavenged scrap and came to believe the old machines could be made to run again. They spent everything on one machine, and it never woke. In the end they sold it for scrap to pay off what they owed.

They grew up in the back streets of a walled city, running errands for a crew of thieves who were the only family they had. The crew was hanged after a job went wrong, and they escaped only because they were late. They left the city that same night.

They were raised in a fishing village on a cold coast, mending nets beside their parents. A raid took the boats and most of the village, and the survivors scattered inland. They went with a handful of them and never saw the coast again.

They fought in the pits for a promoter who kept most of the winnings and all of the fighters. They won their release in a final bout that crippled their opponent. They gave their share of the purse to that fighter's family and walked out of the pits.

They learned to stitch wounds from a traveling doctor who treated anyone, whatever side they fought for. The doctor was killed for treating the wrong side of a feud. They buried the doctor by the road and took the kit, which was all the doctor left.

They were apprenticed to a smith in a busy town and expected to take over the forge one day. The smith left it to a cousin instead. They packed their own hammer and left the town before the cousin took over.

They served a rich family for most of their life and learned every secret behind its walls. When the family lost its power, the servants were thrown out first. The family scattered soon after, and its secrets stopped mattering to anyone.

They grew up in a small cult that waited each year for the end of the world. When the promised day passed in silence, the leader fled with the community's savings. The rest of the cult broke up within a month, and they left with the others.

Beasts overran their town when they were young, and they fled with a handful of other children. They grew up in a refugee camp that no town wanted to take in. The camp broke up when the last of its elders died, and they left to make their own way.

They were jailed for a debt they did not owe and spent years breaking rock in a prison camp. A guard who pitied them looked away during a storm, and they escaped. They crossed the hills before dawn, and the camp never sent anyone after them.

They collected taxes for a local lord and believed the lord kept the roads safe in return. Then they saw raiders paid from the same tax chest to keep the farmers afraid. They threw down their ledger that night and left the lord's lands.

They worked on a hidden farm that grew drugs for the gangs, paid in food and a roof. When a rival gang burned the farm, they ran with a sack of the harvest. They sold it in the next town and used the cats to start over.

When they were young, cannibals overran their village, and they hid for two days under the floor of a burning house. Most of their family did not survive. A passing caravan found them in the ashes and took them to the nearest town.

They rode with a bandit gang for years and did things they would not describe. They left after the gang killed a family that had already handed over everything. A patrol wiped out the gang the next season, and that life ended with it.

They worked for slavers and taught themselves to see the captives as cargo. On one long march, a captive talked to them every night. In the end they cut the captive loose, and the two of them ran in different directions.

They hunted bounties for years and never asked what the targets had done. Their last target turned out to be a parent hiding with a child, and they let them both go. They gave up the reward and the trade that same day.

They farmed land that a lord claimed a share of after every good harvest. They joined a farmers' revolt that the lord crushed in a single season. Most of the other rebels were hanged, and they slipped away in the confusion of the last battle.

They were born into a desert tribe and trained from childhood to fight for its pride. They lost a duel they should have won and were sent away in disgrace. They walked out into the dunes alone and never returned to the tribe.

They grew up as a merchant's child and learned to haggle before they could read. Their parent's caravan was lost with all its goods, and the creditors took everything else. They left the empty family house with the last few cats from the strongbox.
They grew up herding goats on high grassland, far from any town. A drought killed the herd in one bad year. The family split up to find work in the towns, and they went their own way.

They were a guard in a mining town and took pride in keeping order. When the mine owner had striking workers beaten, they were ordered to hold the door, and they did. They handed in their weapon the next morning and left the town.

They trained as a scholar's assistant, copying old texts found in the ruins. The scholar went into a ruin alone one day and never came back. They waited a season, then sold the notes to a collector and moved on.

They were born in a slave camp and knew nothing else until a raid set the camp free. They spent their first free years with the other freed slaves, learning how to choose for themselves. When the group broke up, they set out on their own.
They were a gifted cook in a busy bar until a customer died after a meal. They were blamed, though they believed a rival poisoned the dish. No one was ever charged, and they left that town behind.

They grew up the youngest of many children in a poor farming family, and they left early so there would be one less mouth to feed. They drifted from job to job and never stayed long. Years later they went back once, found strangers working the land, and left without asking.

They hunted wild beasts for their hides and meat and were known as the best tracker for miles around. A hunt went wrong, and their partner died in a beast's jaws while they froze. They sold their gear after the funeral and left the hunting grounds.

They built water pumps and wind generators for the small settlements of the desert. Raiders burned the last settlement they worked for, and their machines with it. They salvaged what parts they could carry and left the desert.

They searched the wasteland for years for a younger sibling taken by slavers. They found the sibling at last, free and settled, and the sibling did not want to know them. They left the sibling in peace and never went looking again.
They raised a child alone and took any job that paid enough to feed them both. The child left one morning to join a mercenary company. A year later, word came that the child had died in a skirmish.

They were the second child of a wealthy family and grew up with servants and fine clothes. A feud between the great families of the city ruined their house. They sold the last of the fine clothes for food and left the city on foot.

They grew up in a town where one gang ran everything, and they joined it as soon as they were old enough. The gang lost a war over the town, and its members were hunted down one by one. They hid in a cellar until the hunt ended, then left the town.

They were a promising student at a fighting school until they broke a rule they thought was unjust. They were cast out, and no other school would take them. They trained alone in the hills for a year and then went down to the towns.

They ran a small bar on a lonely trade road and fed every traveler who came through. Bandits took it over one winter and used it as a camp. They walked away with their life and little else, and the bar burned down in the spring.

They followed a mercenary company as a cook and a tailor for its fighters. The company was wiped out in a battle, and they survived by hiding among the bodies. They took a dead fighter's weapon that day and walked away from the battlefield alone.

They were a prisoner of war, forced to dig fortifications for an army that was not their own. They escaped when the army moved on and left the prisoners to die. The army was broken in its next campaign, and the fortifications they dug fell to ruin.

They were raised under a harsh faith that taught them their kind was lesser. They left at the first chance and found that the rest of the world did not care. The old shame faded over the years, along with the faith.

They spent their youth drunk in a border town, gambling away whatever they earned. After a fight they did not remember, they woke up in a cell. They poured out their last bottle on the day of their release and left that town.

They were a skilled thief who robbed only the rich, and they took pride in never hurting anyone. One job went wrong, and a guard died in the struggle. They left the loot where it lay and gave up thieving that night.

They grew up in a mining family that worked deep underground and rarely saw the sky. A cave-in killed most of the crew, and they were dug out alive after three days. The mine was sealed after the accident, and they left with the other survivors.

They were sent as a child to work for a distant relative in payment of a debt. The relative treated them as a servant until they were old enough to run. They slipped out one night and never saw that household again.

They were a nomad trader who crossed the desert with the seasons. A sandstorm caught their group, and they lost the animals and the goods. The group broke up in the first town they reached, and each member went a separate way.

They raised beasts of burden for the caravans and knew every animal by name. A sickness swept through the pens and killed the whole herd in a month. They burned the pens, sold the land, and closed the business.

They were an enforcer for a moneylender and broke bones for late payments. They quit after they were sent to collect from an old friend. The moneylender was knifed by a debtor a month later, and the matter ended there.

They trained as a guard for a noble house and were chosen to protect its heir. The heir was killed in an ambush on their watch, and the house blamed them. They were dismissed in disgrace, and the ambushers were never found.

They worked on a large estate where the workers were paid in tokens that only the owner's store would take. They ran off with a handful of others, and most of them were caught. They made it out alone and crossed into lands where the owner had no say.

They were born to traveling performers who sang in bars for food. The troupe broke up after a hard winter, and they found themselves alone at a young age. A bar owner took them in for their singing, and they stayed until they were grown.

They grew up in a walled town that always treated them as an outsider because of their race. They left after a mob burned their family's home. The family scattered to other towns, and they set out alone.

They spent years as a grave digger at the edge of a battlefield, burying the dead of both sides. When the war ended, they filled the last grave. They walked away with their shovel and left the battlefield to the grass.

They were a minor gang boss who controlled a single street. A bigger gang took the street and killed most of their people. They escaped over the city wall, and the bigger gang soon lost interest in them.

They were a hired hand on an expedition that went deep into the ruins. Something drove the expedition out, and they would not say what they saw. They sold their share of the relics in the next town, and the expedition broke up.

They were the apprentice of a hermit who taught them to live off the land in the wilds. The hermit died of old age, and they buried the body beside the hut. Then they shut the door of the hut and walked to the nearest town.

They signed up with a mercenary company for the pay and stayed for their comrades. The captain sold the company out to the enemy for a better contract, and half of their comrades died. The captain vanished with the money, and the survivors went their separate ways.
They worked in a bar in a hard town and heard every rumor that passed through. A rumor they repeated got a stranger killed. They left the bar and the town the next morning.
They were a young recruit who dreamed of glory in battle. Their first battle was a slaughter, and they ran before it ended. They threw away their uniform on the road and never went back to the army.

They were taken in by a band of wanderers after their parents died of fever. The band moved from town to town, and they learned a little of every trade. The band broke up when its old leader died, and they went their own way.

They grew up in a slave household and were sold away from their parent at a young age. They escaped years later and went back, but the household was gone. A neighbor told them that the parent had died the winter before.

They were a respected healer in a small settlement until a fever killed half the people there. The survivors blamed them and drove them out. They left with their satchel of herbs and took the first road out of the valley.

They led a small settlement in the wastes and kept it alive through three bad years. A fourth year of drought finished it. They saw the last families off to the towns, then walked away from the empty houses.

They grew up begging in a large city and learned to read people before they learned to read words. A merchant took them on as a runner and taught them the trade. When the merchant died, the heirs sold the business and let them go.

They inherited a small shop from a parent and ran it badly for years. A fire took the shop and every debt with it, and they felt only relief as it burned. They took the road soon after, free of the shop and the debts.

They helped build a great wall around a city, paid in promises that were never kept. Many of the builders died on the work, and the wall was never finished. They left with the last of the builders when the work stopped.

They made crossbows in a workshop that sold to every side of every war. When a customer used their weapons to wipe out a village, they put down their tools. They left the workshop that day and did not return.

They grew up in a farming village that a holy army claimed for its god. The new priests burned the old shrines and took the young for service. They escaped the service on the road and never saw the village again.

They kept lookout for a smuggling ring and spent years watching the roads for patrols. They missed one patrol, and the ring was caught. They were the only one not hanged, and they left that country before the trials were over.

They won so many duels that they were hired to train other fighters. A student they trained went on to lead a bandit gang that raided the roads. A patrol destroyed the gang a year later, and they closed their training yard.

They farmed a small plot until a richer neighbor took it with a crooked deal. They took the matter to the local magistrate and lost there too. They burned the papers that proved the land was theirs and left.

They drew maps for traders and charged well for routes that no one else knew. They sold the same secret route to two rival caravans, and both were ambushed where the route met. They left the trade towns before word of it spread.

They traveled with a group of pilgrims to a holy place that turned out to be an empty ruin. The others went home, but they could not face the journey back. They stayed at the ruin through one season and then set off alone.

They guarded caravans for years and took pride that no cargo of theirs was ever lost. Then one caravan vanished on a road they had chosen, and they alone walked out. The traders paid them off and hired other guards.

They borrowed cats to start a small trade and lost the stock to raiders within a month. The lender made them work the debt off one job at a time, and each job was dirtier than the last. They paid off the last cat after three years and walked away.

They stood guard at the gate of a trade town and knew every face that came through it. One night they let a group of strangers in for a bribe, and the strangers opened the gate to raiders. The town never learned who let them in, and they left its service that winter.
They sold their skill as a mercenary to whoever paid the most. One contract set them against a former comrade, and they carried it out. They took the pay and buried the comrade themselves.

They ran a small repair shop in a busy town and could fix nearly anything brought to the counter. A gang demanded a share of the takings, and they refused. The gang burned the shop, and they left the town with what tools they could carry.

They guarded a remote outpost long after the people who posted them there stopped sending word. When at last they went to look, the settlement that ran the outpost had fallen to ruin. They took down its banner and left the outpost behind.

They were the bodyguard of a wealthy trader and followed the trader from town to town for years. The trader was killed in a crowd while they stood a few steps away, and the killer was never found. The trader's partner paid them off and sent them away.

They hauled loads for a big caravan company and worked its longest routes. The company went under after a string of raids, and the owners fled with the last of the wages. They never saw a cat of that year's pay.

They kept the books for a gang and knew where every cat came from and where it went. When the gang's leaders turned on one another, they took the books and ran. The leaders killed each other within the month, and they dropped the books down a well.

They dug through the ruins with a salvage crew, looking for old technology to sell. The crew found a sealed room, and a fight over what was inside split them apart. They walked away with one strange part and sold it for a few cats in the next town.

They scouted for a wandering band and found it safe paths across the wastes. They led the band into an ambush they should have seen, and few survived. The survivors went their separate ways, and the band ended there.

They were a champion of a fighting ring and won bout after bout for a crowd that loved them. They threw one fight for a bribe, and the crowd never forgave them. They were jeered out of the ring and left the town that night.

They were hired to guard a vault in the desert by a client who paid in advance and never came back. They guarded it for years before they opened it and found it empty. They shut the door again and left the vault to the sand.

They worked for a trader who dealt in stolen goods, and they asked no questions. When the trader was caught, they took the blame in exchange for the promise of a share. They served their time, and the trader died before paying them a single cat.

They served in a town militia that had once been proud of its record. The militia was disbanded after a stronger power took the town, and its members were told to go home. They handed in their badge with the rest and left the town.
They carried orders across the wastes for a minor lord. One message they delivered started a war that ruined both sides. The lord died in that war, and there was no one left to carry messages for.

They fought duels for hire in the place of rich clients who wanted a quarrel settled. They lost a duel that cost their client everything, and the client swore revenge. The client died in poverty a few years later, and the threat died with them.

They woke in a ruined lab with most of their memory gone and no sense of how long they had stood there. They walked out into a world they did not know. Behind them the lab caved in, and every record of who they had been went with it.
They reset their memory centuries ago and left a message for their new self. The message named a place and asked them to go there. They went, found only an empty ruin, and left the message there.

They refused to reset their memory when others of their kind did, and the centuries piled up. The weight of it made them strange even to their own kind, and their companions drifted away one by one. When the last companion left, they walked out of the old city alone.

They stood guard at a post in an age long forgotten. The post fell, and they stood in the dust for a long time before they chose to move. At last they left the ruin and followed a road toward the first town they could see.

They outlived every friend they ever had and buried more of them than they could name. For a long time they kept to themselves to stop the losses. A young traveler broke that long silence, and they walked together until the traveler died of old age.

Soldiers of a holy land hunted them as a demon and cut them nearly to scrap. A traveler with a repair kit put them back together and asked for nothing. The traveler went on their way the next morning, and the two never met again.

They wandered for years on worn joints and failing limbs, because a repair bed cost more than they could pay. They took a hard job to pay for one full repair. They came out of the repair bed whole for the first time in a century.

They spent a long time among their own kind in a dark city, far from the other races. They grew tired of the silence and left to see how the others lived. They climbed out into the light and took the first road they found.

They watched a town grow from a few huts into a city, and then they watched it fall. They stayed through every stage and helped rebuild it twice. When it fell a third time, they left the ruins to the sand.

They saw others of their kind lose their heads to hunters and become mindless thralls. They escaped the same fate by walking through an acid lake where the hunters could not follow. The acid ate at their plating, and they came out on the far side scarred but free.
They traveled for decades with a partner of flesh and watched that partner grow old. The partner died one winter on the road. They buried the partner beside it and walked on alone.

They worked a farm through a drought that drove every other worker away, because they needed no food. The owner left the farm to them before dying, but nothing grew there. They planted for ten more years, then left the farm to the dust.

They grew up on a wheat farm and worked the same fields as their parents. When the parents grew too old for the work, an older sibling took over the farm. With no land of their own to work, they packed a bag and went to find work in the towns.

They spent years carrying water from the town well to the houses of the rich, two buckets at a time. The town built a water pump in the square, and the water carriers lost their trade in a single season. They took their last pay and walked to the next town.

They were apprenticed to a tailor and spent their days mending coats for travelers. The tailor was a fair master, and they learned the trade well. When the apprenticeship ended, the shop had no room for a second tailor, so they left to find their own customers.

They brewed grog in the back room of a small bar and sold every barrel they made. The owner sold the bar to a family that brewed its own. They took their recipe and their copper pot and left the bar to the new owners.

They were a clerk for a trading house and kept its ledgers in a neat hand for years. The trading house moved its business to a bigger town and did not take the clerks along. They closed the last ledger, collected their pay, and left.

They grew cactus on a dry plot at the edge of town and sold the fruit at the market. A run of good years let them save more cats than they ever expected. They sold the plot to a neighbor and set out to see more of the world than one market.

They hauled stone for a builder who put up walls and houses all over a growing town. The town stopped growing, and the builder had less and less work to give. In the end the builder paid them off with a handshake and a good word.

They ran a stall that sold dried meat at a crossroads where caravans stopped to rest. A bigger market opened in a town nearby, and the caravans stopped there instead. They sold the stall for the price of the wood and followed the caravans.

They were the youngest of four children in a family of cooks, and they learned to cook before they could write. Their older siblings took the best jobs in the family kitchen. They left home to cook for strangers, who at least paid for it.
They worked the night watch in a quiet town where nothing ever happened. Years of empty nights wore down their patience. One morning they handed in their lantern and asked for their last pay.
They made rope from hemp in a long shed and sold it to builders and traders. The rope maker who owned the shed retired and closed it. They took a coil of their own rope as a keepsake and moved on.
They worked as a porter at a busy town gate and carried goods for anyone who paid. Their knees gave out after years of heavy loads. They passed the job to a younger porter and left the gate for good.

They grew up in a quiet farming village where every day was much like the last. When they came of age, they took a job with a passing caravan just to see something new. The caravan went far, and they never went back to the village.

They kept the accounts for a group of farmers who sold their harvest together. The farmers argued over prices one season, and the group broke apart. Each farmer went back to selling alone, and no one needed the accounts after that.

They were a cobbler in a small town and mended the boots of half the people there. Their eyes grew weak after years of close work, and they could no longer see the stitches. They sold their awls and lasts to a younger cobbler and closed the shop.

They trained under a doctor in a busy town and spent years stitching cuts and setting bones. The doctor took on a new apprentice who could pay more for the training. They took their kit and set out to work on their own.

They spent most of their youth in their parents' bar, washing cups and listening to travelers. When the parents sold the bar, the new owner brought their own staff. They left with a small share of the sale and the stories of a hundred travelers.

They herded pack animals for a rich farmer and spent long days on the hills with only the animals for company. The farmer sold the herd to pay for a new house in town. Without a herd to watch, they came down from the hills and went looking for other work.

They worked in a mine that dug copper from the hills, and the work was hard but steady. Over the years the seam ran thin and then ran out. The owners closed the mine, and the workers scattered to find new jobs.

They married young and ran a small farm with their partner. After some years they agreed that neither the farm nor the marriage was working. They split the land and the tools fairly, and each went a separate way.

They were a market trader who sold pots and pans from town to town. They grew tired of the same roads and the same haggling. They sold their stock to another trader at a fair price and went in search of a change.

They grew up in a large family in a crowded town house, sharing one room with three siblings. When they were old enough to earn, the house felt too small to stay in. They moved out with a bedroll and a few cats and never moved back.

They baked bread for a small town and were up every morning before dawn. After many years the early mornings wore them down. They sold the oven to a younger baker and slept late for the first time in years.

They spent years as a farmhand on a large estate, planting and harvesting the same fields every season. The estate changed hands, and the new owner brought in workers of their own. They took their last wages and left with the others.

They were a weaver who made cloth for the traders on a long loom in a narrow shop. Traders began to bring in cheaper cloth from far away. They sold the loom, kept their best bolt of cloth, and left the trade.

They worked as a messenger in a big town and ran notes between shops and houses all day. They knew every alley, but the pay never grew. When a caravan offered better pay for a guard, they took the offer and left the town.

They grew up in a fishing village and spent their youth gutting fish on the docks. They hated the smell and never got used to it. They left on the first day they were old enough to go and took a job as far from the water as they could find.

They kept a small inn on a busy road and gave a bed to anyone with a few cats. A bridge was built upriver, and the travelers took the new road across it. Few guests came by after that, and they closed the inn before the money ran out.

They worked in a workshop that made armor plates, and they spent years beating metal into shape. The work left their hands sore and their ears ringing. When the workshop owner retired, they chose not to stay on under the new owner.

They grew up the child of a town guard and expected to join the guard themselves. They tried it for a year and found that they did not like it. They handed back the uniform and left to find a trade that suited them better.

They spent a few years as the cook for a road crew that repaired the trade roads. The crew finished its last road, and the money for new work ran out. The crew broke up, and they went back to the town where the crew began.

They lived in a small town their whole life and knew every family by name. Over the years their friends moved away one by one to bigger places. In the end they followed the last of them out of the town.

They ran errands for a rich old trader who paid well and talked a lot. The trader died peacefully of old age and left them a small sum. They used the cats to buy a good pair of boots and took to the road.

They farmed rice in a wet valley and spent their days knee deep in water. A dry year turned the valley to cracked mud, and the next year was no better. They gave up on rice and left the valley to look for steadier work.

They grew up the child of a shopkeeper and spent their youth behind the counter. When the shop passed to an older sibling, there was no place left for them. They left the shop on good terms and set out to make their own living.

They were a builder's helper and spent years mixing mortar and carrying bricks. The builder fell ill and could no longer work, and the crew was let go. They kept the trowel the builder gave them and moved on.

They worked in a dye shop and spent years with their hands stained blue and red. The owner moved the business to a city where they had no wish to live. They stayed behind, washed their hands one last time, and looked for new work.
They sold water at a desert well to thirsty travelers. A new well was dug in a nearby town, and the travelers stopped coming. They closed the stall and went to the town with the new well.

They worked the counter of a general store and knew the price of every item on the shelves. The owner caught them reading on the job once too often and let them go. They left without hard feelings and took the book with them.

They served drinks in a bar for many years and learned to settle arguments before they turned into fights. The owner decided to retire and sold the place to a rival. The rival wanted their own people behind the bar, and they were let go.

They grew up on a small farm with parents who taught them to read the weather and the soil. The parents grew old and moved into town to live with a relative. The farm was sold, and they set out with their share of the money.

They were a junior clerk in the office of a minor lord and copied letters all day. They grew bored of copying the words of other people. When the season's pay came, they took it and left without a word to anyone.

They spent years picking cotton in hot fields for a big landowner. The work was dull, but the pay was steady. They grew tired of the heat after many seasons, and one morning they did not go back to the fields.
They kept a small green garden alive for a rich family in a dry town. When the family moved away, the new owners let the garden go to dust. They left with a pouch of seeds from the old beds.

They hunted game and sold hides and meat at the market of a small town. Game grew scarce as more hunters came to the area. They sold their traps and their skinning knives and looked for work that was less crowded.

They grew up the child of two merchants and spent their youth on the road between markets. Their parents settled down in one town when they grew tired of travel. They did not want to settle yet, so they took to the road alone.

They spent years as the cook of a merchant's caravan and fed twenty mouths every night. The merchant retired and sold the pack animals. The crew went their separate ways, and they kept the merchant's old cooking pot.

They were a stable hand for the pack animals of a trading post and slept in the hay most nights. The trading post closed when its owner moved away. They found homes for the animals they liked most and left on foot.

They were a clerk who counted grain at the granary of a small town. A new lord took over the town and brought clerks of their own. The old clerks were sent home with a season's pay, and they were one of them.

They made furniture in a small workshop and were known for chairs that never wobbled. A candle fell over one night, and the workshop burned, though nobody was hurt. Rather than build it again, they sold the land and moved on.

They spent their youth as a runner for a market trader, hauling sacks between the stall and the storeroom. The trader taught them to count and to haggle. When the trader closed the stall to marry and move away, they set off to use what they had learned.

They worked as a field hand for a family that treated them like one of their own. The children of the family grew up and took over the work. With no work left for them, the family gave them a good meal and a warm send-off.

They lived for years in the same rented room above a bar, working small jobs around the town. The landlord sold the building, and the new owner raised the rent. They packed their few things and moved on rather than pay it.

They were a well digger who went from village to village to find water underground. They dug their last well for a village that paid them in food for a month. After that well, they decided that they had dug enough holes for one life.

They kept a small shrine clean for the priests of a quiet town. The priests moved to a bigger temple in another town and did not need them. They swept the shrine one last time and left the keys with a neighbor.

They grew up in a mining town and swore as a child that they would never work in the mines. They worked in a shop, a bar, and on a farm instead, and none of the jobs lasted long. When they had tried every job in town, they left to try the jobs in other towns.

They taught children to read and count in a small town for several years. As families moved away, there were fewer children each season. When the last class ended, they closed the schoolroom and left.
They were a barber who cut hair and pulled teeth in a market town. A barber with a steadier hand opened a chair next door. They lost most of their customers to the rival and gave up the trade.

They spent a few years as a guard at a quiet trading post where nothing much happened. The post hired a bigger company of guards, and the old ones were let go. They took their pay and walked to the next town.

They were raised by a grandparent who ran a small rice stall. The grandparent died peacefully in their sleep one winter. They sold the stall to pay for the burial and left the town with what was left.

They spent years as a carpenter's apprentice, building roofs and doors. They fell from a roof and broke a leg, and it healed crooked. Unable to climb, they gave up carpentry and left to find a trade with both feet on the ground.

They counted sacks of grain in and out of a storehouse for a group of traders. One season the numbers did not add up, and they were let go though they had done nothing wrong. They took it as a sign to try something new.
They worked for a sake brewer and spent years stirring the vats. The brewer's own children came of age and needed the jobs. They left with a small cask as a parting gift.

They lit and trimmed the street lamps of a large town every night for years. The town hired fewer lighters to save cats, and they were among the first to go. They left the town on the first night they had no lamps to light.
They looked after the children of a busy merchant family. The children grew up and no longer needed looking after. The family thanked them, paid them well, and they moved on.

They farmed with a partner who was also their closest friend. The friend wanted to stay on the farm for good, and they wanted to see the world. They sold their half of the farm to the friend and parted on good terms.

They worked as a guide who led travelers through the hills to the next town. A safe road was built through the pass, and travelers no longer needed a guide. They walked the new road once to see it and kept on walking.

They spent a season at a desert outpost selling supplies to travelers, and the season turned into five years. The owner of the outpost decided to sell. They took the chance to leave before another five years passed.

They worked in the kitchen of a lord's house and cooked fine meals for guests they never met. The lord moved to a house in another city. They were offered a place in the new kitchen, but they chose to stay behind and leave service.
They made hats of woven straw for the farmers of a dry valley. Fewer farmers worked the valley each year, and fewer hats sold. They wove their last hat for themselves and left the valley wearing it.

They sold dumplings from a cart at the gate of a busy town. They saved enough over the years to buy a small house, but they found that they hated sitting in one place. They sold the house and the cart and took to the road.

They were a gate guard at a quiet trade town and checked the same faces every day for years. The town hired a new captain who brought in guards of their own. They handed in their badge and left without trouble.

They hauled cargo for a small trading company and walked the same route for years. A bigger company bought it and gave the route to its own haulers. They took their pay and found that they had nowhere they had to be.
They kept the stock list of a large warehouse and knew where every crate was kept. The owner sold the warehouse to a trader who kept their own records. They left with their last pay and a clean list.

They worked a forge in a busy town and made plain tools for farmers, such as hoes and picks. Demand fell after a few poor harvests, and the forge closed. They sold the anvil and left to find work elsewhere.

They did repairs for a small town, fixing doors, roofs, and fences for anyone who asked. A larger town nearby took most of the trade, and the small town emptied slowly. They fixed the last loose door on their way out.

They stood watch at a quiet mine for a company that paid on time and asked little. The company sold the mine to a new owner who brought guards of their own. They watched the last of the old crew leave, then left behind them.

They were a courier who carried letters and small parcels between the towns of one region. More traders began to carry letters for a few cats, and the work dried up. They delivered one last parcel and did not come back for another.

They worked as a bouncer at a busy bar and stopped more fights than they could count. The bar changed owners, and the new owner hired a crew of their own. They left with their pay and a few friends among the regulars.

They spent years as a hired hand on a large farm, doing the heavy work that others avoided. The owner sold the land to a neighbor who needed fewer hands. They left with the rest of the workers at the end of the season.
They ran a small shop that sold scrap and spare parts. Business was steady but slow, and the years blurred together. One morning they locked the door, sold the stock to a rival, and left.
They kept lookout from a tower above a farming village, watching for raiders who rarely came. The village built a wall, and the tower was torn down. They helped take it apart and then left.

They kept a trading post open in a quiet corner of the wastes, selling supplies to the few who passed. Fewer and fewer travelers came, and the post stopped paying for itself. They closed it, boarded the windows, and walked away.
They were a sparring partner at a fighting school and took more hits than anyone. The school closed when its old master retired. They left with the other students and went their own way.

They kept the accounts of a mercenary company and paid out the wages every month. A long peace left the company without contracts, and it disbanded. They paid out the last wages, then took their own and left.

They broke rocks at a quarry that supplied stone for the towns. The quarry owner sold the land, and the new owner farmed it instead. They left with the quarry crew when the last stone was carried away.
They worked on a salvage crew that took apart old buildings for their metal. The crew stripped the last building in the area. With nothing left to salvage, the crew broke up.

They built and repaired the fences of a large farm. They finished the last fence of a new field, and the farm had no more fences to build. The owner paid them in full, and they left in search of new work.

They kept the gate of a small town for longer than anyone could remember. The town grew, and a new gate was built on the other side. They locked the old gate one last time and walked out through the new one.

They worked in a library of old books, copying the pages that were falling apart. When the last of the books had been copied, the keeper had no further need of them. They left with one copy that no one else wanted.
They spent decades as a porter in a busy town, because they never grew tired. The town grew rich enough to buy pack animals. They set down their last load and left the work to the animals.

They worked for a long time in a repair shop that served others of their kind. After many centuries, the owner decided to close the shop and rest. They helped pack up the tools and set out with a few spare parts.

They worked the bellows of a forge for a smith who never let them touch the hammer. After many years the smith's hands grew too weak, and the smith closed the forge. They took the bellows as their share and left.

They tutored the children of one family for three generations. The youngest of the fourth generation grew up and had no more need of a tutor. The family gave them a farewell dinner that they could not eat, and they left.

They stood in the same market for decades and sold the same tools to the same families. The families moved away one by one, and the market shrank to a few stalls. They sold the last of the tools and left the empty square.

They worked a water pump by hand for a small village for decades, because they needed no rest. The village bought a wind generator, and the pump was no longer needed. They oiled their own joints, said goodbye, and left.

They spent a long time doing nothing at all in an old ruin, watching the seasons change. One day they decided that they had watched enough. They walked to the nearest town, out of curiosity more than need.
They worked as a night guard for a trader, because they needed no sleep. The trader retired after many years and sold the shop. They were paid off with a sum that would have fed a person for a year.
They sorted scrap in a junk yard and set aside the parts that could be used again. A trader bought the yard and wanted only the metal, melted down. They took the parts that they had saved and left.

They kept the records of a town council for longer than any member served. A new lord replaced the council and kept no records. They packed the old records into crates, left them in a cellar, and left.
